transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Could you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, thank you for seeing me. Um, I guess I'm here because... well, I've just been walking around with this really flat, heavy feeling for a really long time now. It's hard to explain, but it's just this constant weight. And the thing is, I'm a management analyst, so my day-to-day is pretty structured, and honestly, work is going okay. I mean, it's a lot of data and reports, but the people there are actually really nice to me. My coworkers are supportive, there's no major drama or anything at the office that should be dragging me down. 

But even with all that, even when things are perfectly fine on paper and people are being great, I still just feel down. Like, really down and kind of empty most days. I keep trying to figure out why, analyzing it like I do with my projects at work, you know? But there's no logical reason for it. I just sit at my desk and feel this emptiness, and it doesn't matter if someone brings in coffee or if I get a good review from my boss, the heavy feeling is just always there, in the background, coloring everything. It's been going on for so long that I finally thought I should probably talk to someone about it, because I'm just so tired of walking around feeling this empty all the time.
How long have you been feeling this way, with that heavy and empty feeling most days?

Well, if I really track it back... it's been a really long time. Specifically, I'd say it's been right about two years and two months. I know that sounds weirdly exact, but, you know, being an analyst, I kind of map my life out by project quarters and deliverables. And two years and two months ago was exactly when we launched this massive dashboard project at my company. 

It was this huge initiative, and because I was the one building out the reporting structures, it kind of thrust me right into the spotlight. Suddenly all the upper management folks were looking at my work, my name was on all these major email chains, and people were constantly coming up to my desk to congratulate me. And logically, you'd think that would feel amazing, right? Like, I was only twenty at the time, getting all this visibility without even having finished my degree yet. 

But instead of feeling proud or excited, that is exactly when this whole... this heavy, flat emptiness just kind of settled over me. I remember sitting in the final launch meeting, everyone is clapping and smiling, and I just felt completely hollow inside. I kept telling myself that once the post-launch phase was over, the pressure would drop and I'd feel normal again. But then a month passed, and then six months, and now here we are two years and two months later, and that exact same heavy feeling from the dashboard project just never left. It just unpacked its bags and stayed, and I've been dragging it to work with me every single day since.
Have you noticed a time when you felt a clear change in your mood, like feeling down most of the day, nearly every day, or when things you used to enjoy no longer gave you pleasure?

A clear change? Um... no, not really. Not beyond what I just mentioned about it starting two years ago. Like, there hasn't been a specific moment since then where things suddenly got worse, or a time where I woke up and felt like my mood took a massive nosedive. It's really just been... flat. Unchanging. If I were charting it on a line graph for work, there wouldn't be any major spikes or sudden dips, you know? Just this solid, continuous line hovering right below where 'normal' is supposed to be. 

And as for things I used to enjoy... I don't think I've stopped enjoying them, exactly? Like, I still do my usual stuff. I still play tennis on the weekends with a buddy from when I was taking classes, before I paused my degree to work full-time. And I still go out and grab food with my coworkers. It's not like a light switch flipped and suddenly I hated my hobbies or couldn't find any pleasure in them at all. I still do them, and they're fine. It's just that while I'm doing them, that heavy, hollow feeling is just sitting right there next to me on the court, or at the restaurant. It's always in the background. So, no, I haven't really noticed a clear change or a sudden drop-off in pleasure. It's just been the exact same endless, flat gray every single day without any real variation.
Have you noticed that activities you used to enjoy, like playing tennis or going out with friends, feel less pleasurable than they used to, even if you still do them?

Um, no, I wouldn't say *less* pleasurable. I know it's a subtle distinction, but if we're looking at the variables, the actual enjoyment of the activity hasn't really decreased. 

Like, take tennis for example. I play with this guy, Dave, who I met in an macroeconomics seminar right before I took my leave of absence from school to take this full-time analyst job. We play at these public courts down by the river, usually on Saturday mornings unless one of us has a crazy Friday night, which honestly isn't often for me these days. And when we're playing, and I hit a really solid cross-court backhand—which is something I've been actively trying to improve for, like, six months now—I still get that rush, you know? That split-second of, 'yes, I did that perfectly.' The mechanics of enjoying the game are still totally intact. It's not like the tennis itself has lost its appeal or feels dull. I still want to win, and I still laugh when Dave completely shanks a volley into the next court over. 

And it's the exact same thing with going out with my coworkers. Like, last Thursday, a group of us went to this trivia night at a pub near the office. We try to do it maybe twice a month to decompress after the bi-weekly reporting cycle. And I was really into it! I knew the answer to this incredibly obscure geography question about landlocked countries that nobody else at the table got, and I felt that little spike of pride. The food tasted good, the conversation was engaging, people were joking around. I wasn't sitting there thinking, 'Wow, this is boring' or 'I'm not having any fun.' I *was* having fun. The pleasure of the activity was definitely there, exactly how it used to be. 

It's just... it's like I'm running two different operating systems at the exact same time. There's the part of me that is playing tennis or answering trivia and genuinely enjoying it, and then there's this background process that is just constantly running this heavy, empty feeling. The fun doesn't cancel out the emptiness, and the emptiness doesn't necessarily delete the fun. They just coexist in this really frustrating way. 

So, no, to answer your question, the activities themselves don't feel less pleasurable at all. It's more about what I'm carrying with me *into* those activities, if that makes sense? Like, I'm still completely enjoying the tennis match, I'm just playing it while wearing a twenty-pound lead vest.
Have you noticed that even when something good happens—like doing well in tennis or enjoying a night out with coworkers—you don’t feel substantially better or uplifted, even for a little while?

Well, actually... no, that's the thing. I *do* feel better when those things happen. It's not like the good moments are broken or anything. 

Like, if we go back to that trivia night I was just talking about. When I got that geography question right, and everyone at the table was cheering—especially Sarah from accounting, who is insanely competitive and usually answers everything before anyone else can even process the question—I felt genuinely uplifted. For that entire round, and honestly for the rest of the night while we were finishing our drinks and splitting the bill, I felt great. The heavy feeling kind of... paused, I guess? Or at least, the positive feeling of winning and being with my friends was loud enough to drown it out completely. I wasn't sitting there feeling hollow while I was celebrating. I was just celebrating.

And it's the same with tennis. If I have a really good rally with Dave, or if I manage to win a set—which, let's be honest, he's got a killer serve, so winning a set is a major accomplishment for me—I feel a legitimate high from it. I'll be walking back to my car, throwing my racket in the trunk, and I feel energized. I feel lighter. I'll even put on some upbeat playlist for the drive home and actually enjoy the music, singing along and everything. I'll think to myself, 'Wow, that was a great morning, I feel fantastic.'

So, yeah, when good things happen, I absolutely do feel substantially better. The mood boost is real, and it works. The problem isn't that I can't feel uplifted... it's just that the uplift doesn't *stick*. It's like... okay, imagine you're inflating a tire that has a slow leak. While you're pumping the air in—while I'm at trivia, or playing tennis, or getting a compliment at work—the tire fills up, and everything looks and functions perfectly. But the second I stop pumping, the second I walk into my empty apartment or sit down at my desk on a Monday morning with no immediate distractions... the air just starts seeping out again. Within a few hours, or maybe by the next day, I'm right back to that flat, heavy baseline. 

But in the moment? And for a little while after? Yeah, I definitely feel better. The good things still feel good, and they still lift me up. It's just... temporary, I guess. I just wish I didn't have to constantly be doing something engaging or successful just to keep the tire inflated, you know? Because the minute the event is over, it's just a matter of time before I'm back to square one. But the uplift itself? Yeah, that definitely happens.
Have you noticed that you feel unusually tired or low on energy, even after getting enough rest or doing things you enjoy?

Tired? Yeah. Actually, yeah, I am. And it's weird because, like I said, I'm not really doing anything crazy that should be draining me this much. I get decent sleep, you know? I’m usually in bed by 11:00, maybe 11:30, and I set my alarm for 7:00 so I have time to shower, grab a coffee, and commute in without rushing. So I’m getting, what, seven and a half, maybe eight hours? That should be plenty of rest for a twenty-two-year-old. I'm not staying up all night partying or whatever. But it just doesn't seem to matter how much I sleep or if I had a really good, relaxing weekend. 

It's like... the mornings are usually okay, I can push through the first few stand-up meetings and get my inbox sorted. But man, by the afternoon? I am just so completely wiped out. It hits me around 2:00 or 3:00 PM, like this massive, invisible wall. 

And it makes everything so incredibly difficult. Even the basic, routine stuff I do every day at work. Like, fixing a simple spreadsheet error—and as an analyst, I basically live in Excel, so I'm used to tracking down broken VLOOKUPs or whatever—but suddenly it feels impossible. Or just finishing up my expense paperwork, which is literally just scanning receipts and matching them to the corporate card statement. It’s mindless, but it feels monumental when that exhaustion sets in. 

And it affects the stuff outside of work, too. I know I talked about tennis earlier, but I also play in this casual indoor soccer league on weeknights sometimes, and just getting myself to soccer when I feel like that... it's a whole ordeal. It honestly feels like I’m dragging my body and my brain through mud. Just thick, heavy mud. 

And it’s not just a physical tiredness, if that makes sense? It’s not like my muscles are sore from a workout. It’s this deep, heavy exhaustion that gets all up in my head, too. The "brain mud" is almost worse than the physical mud, because I’ll be sitting there staring at my monitor, knowing exactly what I need to do to fix a data set, but the energy required to actually move my mouse and type the numbers feels like I'm trying to run underwater. I'll drink another coffee, maybe grab a seltzer from the breakroom, walk around the floor to stretch my legs, but nothing clears it out. The fatigue just sits there. It's just this heavy, muddy exhaustion that completely takes over my whole afternoon, every single day, no matter how much rest I got the night before.
Can you describe your mood on days when nothing particularly stressful or negative happens—does it feel like you're still carrying that low, heavy feeling even on days when things are going well?

Yeah, exactly. Honestly, that’s actually the main reason I finally decided to come in and see someone in the first place. Because it’s been going on for a really long time now, and I’m just so tired of walking around with this flat, heavy feeling all the time. 

And it is exactly like you said—it happens on completely normal, perfectly fine days. Like, just last Tuesday is a perfect example. Nothing stressful happened at all. My morning commute was actually smooth, the train was on time, which almost never happens on my line. And work was going totally okay. I had a review meeting with the senior partners, and they actually complimented this slide deck I had spent the previous week putting together for our quarterly forecasting. My manager was super nice about it, she even bought me a coffee from the good place down the street as a thank you, and everyone in the office was just generally in a good, relaxed mood because the major deadlines were behind us. 

But even with all of that happening—even with work going well and people being genuinely nice to me and recognizing my effort—I still just felt... down. Like, really down and kind of empty. I was sitting at my desk, sipping this nice coffee, looking at an email that literally said "great job on the presentation," and I just felt completely hollow inside. 

It’s so frustrating because logically, I can look at a day like that and know I should be having a good day. There is absolutely no reason for me to feel bad. No one yelled at me, I didn't mess up any data models, my friends aren't mad at me, my bank account is fine. But that low feeling just doesn't seem to care about the facts of the day. It just sits there in my chest, making everything feel kind of gray and muted. So yeah, even on the days where everything is totally fine and there are zero fires to put out, I’m still just walking around with this heavy emptiness most days. It's like it's the default setting my brain is stuck on, and it just doesn't matter what the actual day looks like on paper.
Would you say that your mood has been persistently low for most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years?

Yeah, two years is... actually, it's pretty much exactly that. Maybe a little more, even. If I really sit down and look at the calendar and think about the timeline, it’s been going on for about two years and two months. 

It’s funny you mention that specific timeframe, because I can actually pinpoint almost exactly when it started. It was right around the time this massive dashboard project wrapped up at work. I was still pretty new to the firm back then, just trying to find my footing, and they gave me this huge assignment to build a real-time tracking dashboard for the regional directors. I mean, I practically lived at the office for a month getting the data integrations to work correctly, pulling in all these different metrics from different departments. 

And it ended up being this huge success, which sounds great, right? But it completely put me in the spotlight. Suddenly, all these senior managers and partners who didn't even know I existed were emailing me directly, asking me to present my reporting in these high-level strategy meetings. I was just a junior analyst, and suddenly everyone was looking at me. 

And honestly, ever since that project put me in the spotlight... that’s when this whole low feeling started. It’s like, you'd think I’d be thrilled about the recognition, and maybe I was for a split second, but then this heavy, flat feeling just kind of rolled in. I kept telling myself it was just post-project burnout, you know? Like, 'Oh, I'm just tired from working so many hours on the dashboard, I'll bounce back next week once things quiet down.' 

But next week came, and the week after that, and the month after that... and the feeling just never left. The spotlight kind of stayed on me, the expectations went up, and that heavy emptiness just unpacked its bags and moved in permanently. So, yeah, it’s been most of the day, more days than not, for two years and two months now. I kept waiting for it to finally lift, because the dashboard project is ancient history at this point and we've moved on to a dozen other things, but I just can't seem to shake it. It's just been there, every day, ever since.
Have you had days where you felt completely fine and free of that heavy, empty feeling at all over the past two years?

I... man, I really don't think so. I'm not sure, honestly, but I haven't noticed any days like that. If I try to scan back through my memory—and I live by my Outlook calendar, so I can literally picture the weeks and months going by—I just don't see any gaps where this heavy feeling wasn't there. 

Like, I try to think of times when I absolutely should have felt completely free of it. For instance, last summer, a buddy of mine from that indoor soccer league organized this weekend trip up to a cabin near a lake. It was supposed to be this totally unplugged weekend, you know? No spreadsheets, no senior partners emailing me at 8:00 PM asking for revised projections. We had a grill going, we were hanging out on the deck, the weather was actually perfect... and I remember sitting there, looking out at the water, and just realizing that the mud was still there. That heavy, empty feeling had just packed itself right into my duffel bag and come to the cabin with me. 

So even on a day like that, where everything was objectively great and I was miles away from the office, I wasn't free of it. It was still just sitting right there in my chest, making everything dull. I mean, you'd think out of over seven hundred days, there'd be at least one where I woke up and just felt light, right? But I really haven't noticed a single day where it completely lifts. It’s always humming in the background, at the very least. So, yeah, I don't think I've had a day where I felt completely fine. If I did, I definitely don't remember it.

Within a few hours, or maybe by the next day, I'm right back to that flat, heavy baseline. 

But in the moment? And for a little while after? Yeah, I definitely feel better. The good things still feel good, and they still lift me up. It's just... temporary, I guess. I just wish I didn't have to constantly be doing something engaging or successful just to keep the tire inflated, you know? Because the minute the event is over, it's just a matter of time before I'm back to square one. But the uplift itself? Yeah, that definitely happens.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a loss of energy or increased fatigability, which would help differentiate between persistent depressive disorder (F34.1), other specified depressive disorder (F34.8), and other potential conditions.
doctor.question: Have you noticed that you feel unusually tired or low on energy, even after getting enough rest or doing things you enjoy?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: By the afternoon I’m so wiped out that even fixing a spreadsheet error, finishing expense paperwork, or getting myself to soccer feels like I’m dragging my body and my brain through mud.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about feeling unusually tired or having low energy despite rest, which corresponds to the Fatigue symptom.

patient.answer:
Tired? Yeah. Actually, yeah, I am. And it's weird because, like I said, I'm not really doing anything crazy that should be draining me this much. I get decent sleep, you know? I’m usually in bed by 11:00, maybe 11:30, and I set my alarm for 7:00 so I have time to shower, grab a coffee, and commute in without rushing. So I’m getting, what, seven and a half, maybe eight hours? That should be plenty of rest for a twenty-two-year-old. I'm not staying up all night partying or whatever. But it just doesn't seem to matter how much I sleep or if I had a really good, relaxing weekend. 

It's like... the mornings are usually okay, I can push through the first few stand-up meetings and get my inbox sorted. But man, by the afternoon? I am just so completely wiped out. It hits me around 2:00 or 3:00 PM, like this massive, invisible wall. 

And it makes everything so incredibly difficult. Even the basic, routine stuff I do every day at work. Like, fixing a simple spreadsheet error—and as an analyst, I basically live in Excel, so I'm used to tracking down broken VLOOKUPs or whatever—but suddenly it feels impossible. Or just finishing up my expense paperwork, which is literally just scanning receipts and matching them to the corporate card statement. It’s mindless, but it feels monumental when that exhaustion sets in. 

And it affects the stuff outside of work, too. I know I talked about tennis earlier, but I also play in this casual indoor soccer league on weeknights sometimes, and just getting myself to soccer when I feel like that... it's a whole ordeal. It honestly feels like I’m dragging my body and my brain through mud. Just thick, heavy mud. 

And it’s not just a physical tiredness, if that makes sense? It’s not like my muscles are sore from a workout. It’s this deep, heavy exhaustion that gets all up in my head, too. The "brain mud" is almost worse than the physical mud, because I’ll be sitting there staring at my monitor, knowing exactly what I need to do to fix a data set, but the energy required to actually move my mouse and type the numbers feels like I'm trying to run underwater. I'll drink another coffee, maybe grab a seltzer from the breakroom, walk around the floor to stretch my legs, but nothing clears it out. The fatigue just sits there. It's just this heavy, muddy exhaustion that completely takes over my whole afternoon, every single day, no matter how much rest I got the night before.

inference.note: The patient reports a persistent low mood lasting more than two years, with no significant loss of pleasure in activities, but rather a coexisting heavy feeling that remains in the background. They experience mood improvement in response to positive events, which argues against major depressive disorder (F32.x or F33.x). Dysthymia (F34.1) and other persistent mood disorders (F34.8) remain likely given the chronic, unchanging nature of symptoms. Borderline personality disorder (F60.5) is less likely due to absence of key features such as affective instability, chronic emptiness, or intense interpersonal difficulties. Adjustment disorder (F43.2) is ruled out due to the duration and persistence of symptoms beyond a typical stressor timeline.

doctor.intent: Assess if the patient has a persistently low mood that is not reactive to positive events, which would help differentiate between F34.1 (Dysthymia) and F34.8 (Other Specified Depressive Disorders).
doctor.question: Can you describe your mood on days when nothing particularly stressful or negative happens—does it feel like you're still carrying that low, heavy feeling even on days when things are going well?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: I came in because for a long time now I’ve been walking around with this flat, heavy feeling, like even when work is going okay or people are nice to me, I still feel down and kind of empty most days.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my general mood, specifically the 'low, heavy feeling' even when things are going well, which directly matches my manifestation of a persistent depressed mood.

patient.answer:
Yeah, exactly. Honestly, that’s actually the main reason I finally decided to come in and see someone in the first place. Because it’s been going on for a really long time now, and I’m just so tired of walking around with this flat, heavy feeling all the time. 

And it is exactly like you said—it happens on completely normal, perfectly fine days. Like, just last Tuesday is a perfect example. Nothing stressful happened at all. My morning commute was actually smooth, the train was on time, which almost never happens on my line. And work was going totally okay. I had a review meeting with the senior partners, and they actually complimented this slide deck I had spent the previous week putting together for our quarterly forecasting. My manager was super nice about it, she even bought me a coffee from the good place down the street as a thank you, and everyone in the office was just generally in a good, relaxed mood because the major deadlines were behind us. 

But even with all of that happening—even with work going well and people being genuinely nice to me and recognizing my effort—I still just felt... down. Like, really down and kind of empty. I was sitting at my desk, sipping this nice coffee, looking at an email that literally said "great job on the presentation," and I just felt completely hollow inside. 

It’s so frustrating because logically, I can look at a day like that and know I should be having a good day. There is absolutely no reason for me to feel bad. No one yelled at me, I didn't mess up any data models, my friends aren't mad at me, my bank account is fine. But that low feeling just doesn't seem to care about the facts of the day. It just sits there in my chest, making everything feel kind of gray and muted. So yeah, even on the days where everything is totally fine and there are zero fires to put out, I’m still just walking around with this heavy emptiness most days. It's like it's the default setting my brain is stuck on, and it just doesn't matter what the actual day looks like on paper.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a persistent low mood that meets criteria for dysthymia (F34.1) versus another specified persistent mood disorder (F34.8)
doctor.question: Would you say that your mood has been persistently low for most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about two years and two months, ever since the dashboard project put me in the spotlight at work.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the duration of the persistently low mood, specifically if it has been going on for at least two years, which corresponds to the duration item in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah, two years is... actually, it's pretty much exactly that. Maybe a little more, even. If I really sit down and look at the calendar and think about the timeline, it’s been going on for about two years and two months. 

It’s funny you mention that specific timeframe, because I can actually pinpoint almost exactly when it started. It was right around the time this massive dashboard project wrapped up at work. I was still pretty new to the firm back then, just trying to find my footing, and they gave me this huge assignment to build a real-time tracking dashboard for the regional directors. I mean, I practically lived at the office for a month getting the data integrations to work correctly, pulling in all these different metrics from different departments. 

And it ended up being this huge success, which sounds great, right? But it completely put me in the spotlight. Suddenly, all these senior managers and partners who didn't even know I existed were emailing me directly, asking me to present my reporting in these high-level strategy meetings. I was just a junior analyst, and suddenly everyone was looking at me. 

And honestly, ever since that project put me in the spotlight... that’s when this whole low feeling started. It’s like, you'd think I’d be thrilled about the recognition, and maybe I was for a split second, but then this heavy, flat feeling just kind of rolled in. I kept telling myself it was just post-project burnout, you know? Like, 'Oh, I'm just tired from working so many hours on the dashboard, I'll bounce back next week once things quiet down.' 

But next week came, and the week after that, and the month after that... and the feeling just never left. The spotlight kind of stayed on me, the expectations went up, and that heavy emptiness just unpacked its bags and moved in permanently. So, yeah, it’s been most of the day, more days than not, for two years and two months now. I kept waiting for it to finally lift, because the dashboard project is ancient history at this point and we've moved on to a dozen other things, but I just can't seem to shake it. It's just been there, every day, ever since.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) with symptoms present for at least two years, which would support F34.1 (Persistent mood [affective] disorder), as opposed to F34.8 (Other specified mood [affective] disorders), which may include shorter or less consistent presentations.
doctor.question: Have you had days where you felt completely fine and free of that heavy, empty feeling at all over the past two years?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient has had any symptom-free periods during the two-year duration, which is a specific diagnostic criterion for Persistent Depressive Disorder but is not covered in the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I... man, I really don't think so. I'm not sure, honestly, but I haven't noticed any days like that. If I try to scan back through my memory—and I live by my Outlook calendar, so I can literally picture the weeks and months going by—I just don't see any gaps where this heavy feeling wasn't there. 

Like, I try to think of times when I absolutely should have felt completely free of it. For instance, last summer, a buddy of mine from that indoor soccer league organized this weekend trip up to a cabin near a lake. It was supposed to be this totally unplugged weekend, you know? No spreadsheets, no senior partners emailing me at 8:00 PM asking for revised projections. We had a grill going, we were hanging out on the deck, the weather was actually perfect... and I remember sitting there, looking out at the water, and just realizing that the mud was still there. That heavy, empty feeling had just packed itself right into my duffel bag and come to the cabin with me. 

So even on a day like that, where everything was objectively great and I was miles away from the office, I wasn't free of it. It was still just sitting right there in my chest, making everything dull. I mean, you'd think out of over seven hundred days, there'd be at least one where I woke up and just felt light, right? But I really haven't noticed a single day where it completely lifts. It’s always humming in the background, at the very least. So, yeah, I don't think I've had a day where I felt completely fine. If I did, I definitely don't remember it.
